BFS because calorie counting and tracking is mentally exhausting

I'm not fat, never was but I never counted calories.

What I do is simple. I eat as healthy as possible and avoid processed food. I almost never (maybe twice a year) eat sweets, chocolate and desserts in general. Almost never drink anything else other than water.

I eat when I'm hungry and stop when I'm full. If I'm full and there's even a single bite left on the plate I don't eat it.

Worked well so far, currently 75 kg at 1.80 m.

That is great for maintaining a healthy weight and great advice for a healthy life, but to get back down to a healthy weight I need to create a calorie deficit. Additionally, I see a dietician once a month and have to submit data for us to review. Not a fan of sweets myself, thankfully.

I actually lost 5 kg, down from 80 (my all time high) this way. This may be because I started running and made my workout a little harder or maybe it's just too hot and my appetite is lower.

But yes, the best way is actually counting calories although what I do is a very good start. Most fat people would lose a lot of weight just by eliminating fast food and sweets, drinking only water and exercising.

I'm fat as hell and I've just started changing my eating habits about a month and a half ago. So far, around 20 lbs down and counting, BUT I know there will come a time when I need to reign it in even more and start tracking and counting calories. I'm not looking forward to it because I've done it before and it's so time consuming it ends up being all I think about, which I believe fosters an unhealthy obsession with food. Whether you're eating healthily or unhealthily food should not be everything you think about. It sucks.

Its funny how obsessed you get with the whole calorie counting process. It's not that I am thinking 'I want to eat this and I can't' it's more like 'I don't trust that the chicken salad I just tracked in MFP is the exact same caloric content as the chicken salad I just ate'. Then I get all stressed out.

My band covers an entire album every month live. This one was Neil Young's After the Gold Rush, which is one of my favorite albums. Here is a video of When You Dance I Can Really Love and the 2nd half of the gig. I also made some guitar lessons for most of the songs on the album. Here's the lesson for When You Dance I Can Really Love. It's in DADGBD and it is super fun to play.
My band performed Neil Young's After the Gold Rush in its entirety a couple months ago. Tons of fun to figure it all out. (Video and guitar lesson)

An entire album!?!?!? Seriously!!?? Hats off to you!! That's major ambition! There's no way I could learn songs that fast! I've learned 7 songs in the last month, and one of them doesn't count, because I wrote it. It's been a serious commitment, and if you can give any pointers on how to more quickly memorize songs, it would be appreciated. I can usually memorize the structure and create an arrangement fairly quickly, but not so much the lyrics.

Thank you! It is a lot of work, but we do it by communicating efficiently and delegating parts. We are a six piece band with a dedicated lead singer. That really helps that the lead Vox aren't one of us plowing through all the guitar and keys and bass parts. We did sing 4 part harmony on most of this record though. In this case, it was easy for me to remember the lyrics because it is one of my favorite albums, but we did The Stone Roses last month and I had to do all of the backing Vox (almost as much singing as the lead), as well as the rhythm guitar parts. I usually swap lead with the other guitarist to cut down on time learning the guitar solos, but not that time, too much. We also have a PDF of every song on a one-sheet on iPads attached to our mic stands in case we need them. The best advice I have is to practice A LOT. I play about an hour every day and I've been playing guitar for over 20 years. Focus your attention on learning tonal relationships between chords and notes. For instance, know what a I, V, vi, IV chord progression sounds like and you can identify it in any key. Helps a lot with quickly picking up what is going on in a song. Know the relationships between notes, if you automatically know by hearing an interval that it is a 6th or major 3rd/minor 3rd or whatever you can quickly figure out just about anything, or even just feel it once you identified the key. It gets easier and easier the more you do it until things almost become 2nd nature. Rely less on TABs and more on your ears (unless your ears suck, then work on fixing that). Hope that helps.

I'm old, and while I can recognize and memorize the song structures quickly, it's memorizing lyrics that kills me, as I play guitar and sing for my Celtic band. I also do the arrangements, lead sheets, and scratch recordings for the band to practice. It just took me three days to learn a new song. I had the guitar part down in about 30 mins, The rest of the time was spent memorizing the lyrics and polishing the rough edges. I really hate memorizing lyrics!

I have a lot of trouble with lyrics sometimes too. I write music too and my wife jokes that I often have to read her lips when she's in the front of one of my shows to remember them. I highly recommend getting a tablet you just load your lyrics into and having it fixed to your mic stand. It isn't super noticeable and you can glance down quickly if you need to. I practice with my song sheets up on my iPad on the mic stand all the time.

I actually have an Android tablet that I use with Lyric Pad. Sadly, for the past two months I've been going back and forth with Samsung getting it repaired, and finally replaced. Hopefully I'll have it back next week! Going to rehearsal without it made me realize how well I'd actually managed to memorize most of my set! We're adding songs at a pretty fast clip (For me, anyway) right now, so it's a struggle. Fortunately, the band is great, and the fiddle player is happy to take a few more bars of solo if I forget a lyric. :)

I had a great mentor that said this over and over and over: Repetition is the mother of learning. You can exercise your memory like anything else. Focus on the chorus first and then break up the song verse by verse. So, just memorize the chorus, then keep repeating it out loud. Get it stuck in your head. Then repeat for each section of the song. Break them up into manageable chunks, then it's a lot easier to put it all together.

I'm finding this to be what works best for me.. I probably need twice the repetition as the next guy! I usually repeat verse/chorus until I have it, the add the next verse, then the next... Someone suggested I try writing it out on paper by hand, then typing it back in.. That didn't work as well for me as just repeating verses for days on end until it sticks. Fortunately, I can usually get the guitar parts down in a few minutes, but the lyrics take days. Part of it is probably that with our genre of music, every song is like a novel, and some of the vernacular can be a bit archaic. Fortunately, the guitar parts are simple and repetitive, and often times the chords don't change for the chorus.
